title: Groundhog Pod: Scaling AI Inference with Kata Pod Snapshots
tldr: Microsoft extended Kata Containers and Cloud Hypervisor to snapshot a whole pod VM, including GPU state captured with CUDA checkpoint, after the model is loaded. Restoring from the snapshot cut a demo inference pod's time to first response from about 34 seconds to about 11.

key_points.text: Slow inference pod startup (image pull, loading Python, PyTorch and CUDA, loading weights, warm-up) costs money while serving nothing.
Startup latency sets how many warm pods you keep in reserve for spikes; faster startup means a smaller buffer.

CRIU checkpoints a process and its memory but not kernel state. Kata runs each pod in a lightweight VM with its own guest kernel, so a VM snapshot captures application, CPU, memory and kernel state together.

Snapshots fail to restore across CPU microarchitectures; a virtual CPU profile with a minimum feature set lets a snapshot taken on one CPU generation restore on another, leaving GPU compatibility as the main constraint.
GPU memory and execution state are captured with CUDA checkpoint into guest RAM, and then the whole VM is snapshotted to a storage back end.
Restore: an annotation on the pod tells the Kata runtime to start the VM from the snapshot, then CUDA checkpoint restores and unlocks the GPU.
Demo with a Pythia text-generation model: after snapshotting, the running pod resumed inference, was terminated, and a new pod restored from the snapshot answered in about 11 seconds.
From the snapshot, the software and model loading steps are skipped; GPU warm-up takes slightly longer.

Snapshots also help with traffic spikes, worker failures, quiet periods, group and batch jobs, Java JIT warm-up, and ML training, where a demo resumed the loss curve after restoring a mid-training snapshot.
Some Cloud Hypervisor changes are upstream; Kata snapshot and restore design is in progress, with plans to align with open KEPs in SIG Node and containerd work on snapshot/restore.
Q&A: no cross-architecture restore (for example ARM to AMD64); same-architecture restore works on tested SKUs and depends on the CPU feature profile, and GPU compatibility will be limited at first.

numbers.text: Demo cold start took about 33 to 34 seconds to a response; restore from snapshot took about 11 seconds, about a 65% improvement.
Loading software and model took about 21 seconds cold versus 5 seconds from a snapshot.
CPU-only restores reach sub-second restart times in their lab.
A simulation with pay-as-you-go H200 pricing saved about $30 over 3 minutes 45 seconds of spiky traffic.

open_gaps.text: The demo pins to and restores on a single GPU; restoring across GPUs needs more work.
Results were on a modest GPU with no optimizations; restore speed, CUDA recovery paths and snapshot size still need tuning on production hardware.
Protecting snapshots in multi-tenant clusters and using confidential containers to hide models from the infra provider are open.
GPU compatibility between snapshot and restore hosts is a big unresolved question.

opportunities.text: Join the upcoming upstream Kata snapshot and restore design work announced on the Kata Slack.
Follow the SIG Node KEPs and containerd proposals for snapshot/restore that Kata plans to integrate with.
Model your warm-pod buffer as a function of startup latency to estimate savings from faster restores.
Test mid-training VM snapshots as a way to survive evictions and maintenance without restarting jobs.
